bearings.paper_claim: Organizations that lobby and organizations that give through PACs barely overlap. Per year, as a share of all politically active organizations: 1998 (n=9,076) 64% lobby only, 24% PAC only, 12% both; 2008 (n=15,729) 70/20/10. Pooled 1998-2018 (Figure 4): 3,427 organizations (6.3%) did both; the 6.3% is printed, and its denominator 54,517 is the sum of the four Figure 4 groups (34,038 only lobby, 9,528 only contribute, 3,427 both, 7,524 not active), so it includes inactive organizations. The authors put the yearly overlap at 10-15% and tell researchers not to conflate lobbying and electioneering.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.597; Results pp.600-601; Figure 4 p.603; Implications pp.603-604
bearings.system_side: Bridge round 3 (look dated 2026-08-01) is CLOSED and UNCORROBORATED: pooled member-level Spearman rho +0.153 (p=0.015) but four-control partial -0.0002, window 2023-2026, pooled N=213 member x industry x cycle pairs from fintech and crypto, two cycles each (credit_union strata coverage-limited and not entering). Fixed consequence wording: FEC exposure is a target-side money prior only and must not be presented as a lobbying-relationship predictor. The LDA side uses a locked 22-lob_id crosswalk.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about organizations; the bridge is about members (where money exposure and lobbying attention land). Different estimands, and the paper does not explain the zero partial. What carries over is the population point: organizations that lobby without a PAC (64-70% of all politically active organizations per year, about 84-88% of lobbying organizations) leave no organizational FEC trace, so FEC cannot be a general lobbying proxy. Federal organizations, 1998-2018, CRP definitions. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers all confirmed in text (lines 324-331, 444, 598, Figure 4 counts, 10-15% at p.604). Bridge numbers are not at bridge3_look.py:27-40 (that is config); they are in fec_lda_bridge3_prereg.md RESULT-BRIDGE3 and match (rho +0.152525809416, partial -0.000204468398, N=213, fintech 48+55, crypto 44+66). Removed the analyst's claim that the 22-lob_id crosswalk was 'selected on organizations doing both': nothing found shows the crosswalk was selected on PAC status. Noted that the 54,517 denominator includes 7,524 inactive organizations.

bearings.paper_claim: Among all politically active organizations, 64-70% per year lobby without making PAC contributions; among lobbying organizations alone that is roughly 84% (1998) to 88% (2008). The share of PAC contribution dollars coming from organizations that also lobby fell from more than 65% (1998) to about 30% (2018). Contributions by employees or contract lobbyists are not counted as organizational giving.
bearings.paper_location: Results pp.600-601 (Figure 1 and Figure 2 text); Data and Methods p.599
bearings.system_side: The 'FEC leads LDA' heuristic number comes from _lead_months, computed as months from the end of the LobbyView finance-joined filing year to the latest FEC transaction date: a data-freshness gap, not an estimated lag. The opposition prior's FEC basis is itemized individual giving by employees and executives of 10 sample companies per industry plus limited corporate rows, not industry-complete.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Low overlap undercuts any reading in which one organization's giving foreshadows its own later lobbying, because most lobbying organizations do not give through a PAC. The paper measures organizational/affiliated-PAC money, not the employee giving this prior uses, so it bounds the lead wording rather than refuting it. The freshness reading of lead_months is unaffected. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: The analyst wrote 'most lobbying organizations make no PAC contributions (64-70% lobby only)'. The 64%/70% shares are of all politically active organizations, not of lobbying organizations; corrected (64/(64+12)=84%, 70/(70+10)=88%). The 65%->30% figure is confirmed at text line 404. Code side confirmed: _lead_months at 564-572 and its use at 1567; the 10-companies employee/executive basis is stated at build_opposition_prior.py:108.

bearings.paper_claim: About 75% of 1998-2018 lobbying expenditures came from organizations that also gave through PACs. The top lobbying groups almost always have affiliated PACs. Organizations doing both average $403,435 a year in lobbying (IQR $118,825-$1,558,597) vs $64,000 for lobby-only organizations (IQR $30,000-$130,000). Even so, 64-70% of politically active organizations per year lobby without a PAC.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.597; Results p.601 (Figure 2a, Figure 3b text)
bearings.system_side: In pflip the opposing side b = WM*pm*(cm*ind+1)/((cm*ind+1)+HALFF*R) + WP*nB/mBt: an opposing-industry money leg built from ind0 = banks + finserv from congestion.json (industry PAC money), saturated against member receipts, plus a peer/network leg. WM=0.35, WP=0.65. No lobbying-spend term enters b.
bearings.transfer_conditions: PAC money should flag the biggest lobbying spenders, since the paper finds those almost always have PACs; organizations that lobby without a PAC contribute nothing to b's money leg. Whether specific finance opponents (ABA, ICBA, large banks, fintech or crypto firms) fall in either group is the analyst's assumption, not in the paper. The paper tests neither access nor votes and gives no support for the WM/WP split. UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper figures confirmed (lines 400-404, 432-436). Corrected the 64-70% denominator (all politically active organizations, not lobbying organizations) and dropped 'Implications p.602' as a location for these facts. Code: ind0 is at line 39 (imputation through 47), WM/WP at 21, and b is defined at 96; b also has a peer leg (WP*nB/mBt), so 'only as PAC money' holds for the money leg only. congestion.json being industry PAC money is stated at build_opposition_prior.py:113. Line 21's own comment cites Kalla & Broockman for 'money buys access'; this paper does not support that.

bearings.paper_claim: Organizational giving is campaign donations from the organization or its officially affiliated PAC; contributions by employees and contract lobbyists are not counted. Dark-money contributions are not observed. Independent expenditures (often by Super PACs) are not discussed; the article covers contributions to candidates only.
bearings.paper_location: Data and Methods p.599; note 1 p.604
bearings.system_side: Mentat attributes FEC receipts to roster companies by normalized key, using contributor_employer for individual contributions and contributor_name otherwise, with legal-suffix and bank N.A. stripping on employer keys, so its company giving includes individual employee giving the paper excludes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Comparing Mentat industry totals or participation counts with the paper's overlap or distribution figures requires restricting Mentat to organizational and affiliated-PAC receipts first. Melange's opposition prior already records that employee/executive giving and industry PAC money (congestion.json) are different instruments, with lean signs agreeing for only 157/276 members (57%) (fec/lobbying/build_opposition_prior.py:113).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side confirmed (text lines 293-302, note 1 at 692-697). Note: Figure 3a text names Crossroads GPS, Restore Our Future and Priorities USA among the largest contributors, which sits awkwardly with the stated candidate-contributions-only scope; that is the paper's issue. Code: the employer-vs-name switch is at collect.R:71, which the analyst omitted; 363-380 is only employer-key normalization. The 57% (157/276) figure was cited to a 'precognition memo'; it is confirmed at build_opposition_prior.py:113.

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying and PAC spending have different distributions: lobbying spenders concentrate between $10,000 and $1 million and few disclose under $10,000, while PAC giving is more uneven, with many groups giving under $10,000. A PAC contribution can be one-off, while hiring a lobbyist stretches over months or years. The authors argue the umbrella term 'money in politics' is imperfect and that researchers should say which type they study.
bearings.paper_location: Implications, Public Discourse p.602; Research p.603
bearings.system_side: Mentat's giving forecast passes Melange LDA levels to the lobbying card separately from the giving model, with outside-firm income (hired_firms) and in-house expenses shown side by side and never added.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports keeping giving and lobbying as separate measures with separate models. It does not speak to the in-house vs outside-firm no-sum rule, which is about LDA double counting; the paper says only that its lobbying totals include both in-house and contracted-firm spending and does not describe deduplication. Mentat's sector growth study config separately records a median 9-26% double count in undifferentiated LobbyView sums (C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/sector_growth_study/code/R/sgs_config.R:118-120). Descriptive evidence only.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side confirmed (text lines 500-516, 561-562). Code confirmed at giving_forecast.py:552-562 ('never added here'). Removed the analyst's statement that 'CRP data does deduplicate that': the paper does not say so. Corrected the sgs_config.R path (it is under Mentat/sector_growth_study/code/R, not mentat/R).

related.why: Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters study firm-politician dyads among publicly traded US manufacturing firms (2,703 that lobbied or donated, 2008-2018) and test whether donations precede lobbying. Furnas et al. give the population base rate: only 10-15% of politically active organizations per year do both. They do not cite Kim and do not contradict a dyad-level sequencing finding, so this is complementary, not a contradiction.
The later version of the same donations-then-lobbying sequencing argument. Furnas's low overlap bounds how much of the organizational population such sequencing can describe.
Furnas et al. cite Kalla and Broockman 2016 among works resting on the premise that groups contribute to buy access (p.598; reference list).

This item is the 2019 APSA working-paper version of Furnas, LaPira, Hertel-Fernandez, Drutman and Kosar's survey experiment, published as Furnas et al. 2023 (PRQ 76(1)). The PS article cites the 2023 version as contrary experimental evidence on buying access.
Studies corporate lobbying and PACs together in relation to market concentration (per its title). Furnas supplies the base rate for how often organizations use both.

Paul's cross-industry finance and lobbying report sets campaign giving and lobbying side by side for five financial-services industries. Furnas warns that the two come largely from different organization populations and should not be conflated.

This memo mixes executive giving, company PACs, trade associations and Super PACs across four industries. Furnas's definitions (organizational/affiliated-PAC candidate contributions only; employees and Super PAC independent expenditures excluded) set what can be compared.

summary_issues: The pooled '3,427 of 54,517 organizations (6.3%)' is arithmetically right and the 6.3% is printed in the paper, but the 54,517 denominator includes 7,524 organizations Figure 4 labels 'Not Active'. Say so whenever the 6.3% is quoted.

Bearings, gaps_exposed and paul_alignment repeatedly describe 64-70% as the share of 'lobbying organizations' that make no PAC contributions. The paper's 64%/70% are shares of all politically active organizations. Among lobbying organizations the lobby-only share is about 84% (1998) and 88% (2008). summary_md itself uses the correct denominator.
summary_md says the flip model's competitor leg 'counts only PAC money'. b also has a peer/network leg (WP*nB/mBt, flip_model.py:96); only its money leg is PAC money.

rel cites the bridge round-3 numbers to fec_lda_bridge3_look.py:27-40, which holds only config. The results are in fec_lda_bridge3_prereg.md RESULT-BRIDGE3 (lines 272-290). The claim that the 22-lob_id crosswalk was selected on dual-activity organizations is unsupported and was removed.

rel says CRP data deduplicates in-house vs outside-firm lobbying. The paper does not say this; it says only that both are included. The sgs_config.R path is also wrong (it is C:/Users/pgoff/Mentat/sector_growth_study/code/R/sgs_config.R).

The related link to kim-2020 was labelled 'contradicts' and said Kim studied 'large firms'. Kim's sample is all publicly traded manufacturing firms that lobbied or donated, and Furnas neither cites nor contradicts it. Relabelled to complements. The furnas-2019 item is the working-paper version of the cited 2023 PRQ article, so the link is 'cites', not 'builds-on'.
The analyst's own wording that large finance opponents (ABA, ICBA, big banks) are dual-activity spenders is not from the paper. Treat it as an assumption.
